title: Played dead, flew free
hook: the caged parrot copies it, is thrown out of the cage, and flies (Masnavi 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the arrow: a spoken word can't be called back. A wild parrot heard the caged one's greeting and fell from the tree.

Plenty of people have a version of themselves they perform. The funny one at parties. The one who's always fine. The high achiever, the helper, the cool one who doesn't care. Maybe it started as a gift, and people loved it. Then slowly it became a cage, because now you have to keep performing, or they won't love you anymore. The merchant is home. His parrot has asked what happened in India. Ashamed, he tells it: a wild parrot heard your greeting, trembled, and fell down dead. Today, played dead.
screen: `THE SELF YOU PERFORM.` → `A GIFT THAT BECAME A CAGE.` → `PLAYED DEAD.`

segments.voice: As soon as the merchant finishes, his own parrot begins to tremble. It shakes in the cage, falls from its perch, and lies there, stiff and still. The merchant is shattered. He cries out, tears his clothes, and mourns his sweet-voiced bird, the companion of his days; Rumi gives him a long, aching lament. Then, heartbroken, he opens the cage, lifts the little body out, and lets it drop. And the parrot flies, straight up to a high branch, alive and free. What just happened? the stunned merchant calls. The parrot explains. That wild parrot in India wasn't dead. It was sending me advice by what it did: your beautiful voice, your charm, the way you delight everyone, that's what put you in the cage. Let it go. Become as if dead, and you'll be set free. The parrot says a kind goodbye to its master, and flies away. Rumi's lesson: the thing that makes people admire you can be the very thing that traps you. Sufis have a saying for this, which they attribute to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: die before you die. Hadith scholars say it isn't found in the recognized collections, though Sufi teachers treasure it. It doesn't mean harming yourself in any way. It means letting the grasping, performing self fall still, the ego from the lion inside, so that something truer can live. The parrot didn't stop being a parrot. It stopped performing, and it flew. Die before you die.
screen: `THE CAGED PARROT FALLS STILL.` · `THROWN OUT, IT FLIES FREE.` · `YOUR CHARM PUT YOU IN THE CAGE.` · `LET THE PERFORMING SELF FALL STILL.` · then, large: `DIE BEFORE YOU DIE.`

segments.voice: Ask: what do I do mostly so people will like me, or see me a certain way? Always upbeat, always with an answer, pretending not to care; pick one. Imagine letting it go still, not dramatically, just not doing it, and notice what's underneath; it may be tender, and that's all right.
Played dead. The caged parrot copies the wild one, falls still, is thrown out of its cage, and flies free: letting the performing self go. Today's word.
Your line: die before you die. The charm was the cage. That's day one hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Sufi teachers often read the merchant and the parrot as a lesson in fana, the passing away of the ego, and quote the saying 'die before you die' in explaining it.
